title: Introduce yourself
summary: Move through identity, origin, arrival, home, language ability, and first impressions without repeating obvious subjects.
takeaways: から marks origin; に marks the time or destination point.
Japanese naturally drops [[私は|わたしは]] after the topic is clear.
あまり pairs with a negative expression for “not very much.”

grammar.title: Origin and arrival
grammar.pattern: Place から[[来ました|きました]] / Time に[[来ました|きました]]
grammar.summary: Use から for where movement begins and に for the time point or destination.

examples.english: I came to Japan in April.

grammar.title: What you understand takes が
grammar.pattern: Noun が[[分かります|わかります]]
grammar.summary: With [[分かります|わかります]], the understood thing is marked by が, even though English makes it an object.

examples.english: I do not understand very well.

grammar.caution: あまり normally expects a negative ending.

grammar.title: Describe a current state
grammar.pattern: Place に[[住んでいます|すんでいます]]
grammar.summary: The ています form can describe an ongoing state. Here, に marks the place where the person resides.
grammar.caution: Learn this as a useful whole pattern for now; full て-form rules come later.

recall.prompt: How do you say “I came from Chile”?
recall.answer: チリから[[来ました|きました]]。

recall.prompt: Which particle marks the language in [[日本語|にほんご]]＿[[分かります|わかります]]?
